newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Two Serbs reported shot in Kosovo province ambush.
newsitem.headline: Two Serbs reported shot in Kosovo province ambush.

text.p: A police officer and a civil servant, both Serbs, were killed in an ambush in the volatile Serbian province of Kosovo, whichg is populated mainly by ethnic Albanians, Belgrade media reported on Saturday.

"Unknown terrorists fired from automatic weapons and killed Pristina police inspector Milos Nikolic and Podujevo employment office employee Dragan Rakic after 10 p.m. (on Friday) in the village of Surkis, near Podujevo," the daily Politika reported.
It said the attackers were waiting in ambush and opened fire from automatic weapons when Nikolic and Rakic stopped their car in front of Nikolic's house. Rakic was a father of three.
Radio Pristina in the Kosovo capital Pristina said the police had surrounded the village after the killing, the Belgrade news agency Beta reported.

The Democratic League of Kosovo (DLK), which represents Kosovo Albanians, said Serbian police sent a convoy of vehicles from Pristina towards Podujevo. It added that several Albanians were arrested but no official confirmation was available.
Serbian police refused to comment on the case, as did investigative judge Mijat Bajovic at Prokuplje district court.
The LDK said the area remained calm on Saturday but it expressed concern that the situation might deteriorate.
Podujevo Serbs said they would hold a rally on Saturday, the town's market day, to protest the killings, Beta said
"Nikolic has long been the target of Albanian terrorists," the Belgrade newspaper Politika Ekspres said. "Two years ago, they threw a Molotov cocktail at his house in Surkis."
It added that Rakic had been attacked in a room of his home in 1974, when his neighbour, an Albanian, shot him with a carbine. The bullet hit Rakic near the heart.

Serbian police made several arrests earlier this month over a spate of shootings, bombings and arson in the province. Several people, mainly Serbian police, have been killed since the beginning of the year.
Ninety per cent of Kosovo's population are ethnic Albanians.
Belgrade stripped the province of its autonomy in 1989, saying the Albanians wanted to secede from Serbia. Since then, most of the Albanians have rejected Serbian authority.
LDK accuses Serbia of systematic human rights abuses and alleges several Albanians were tortured to death or killed in the hands of the police.
In a landmark deal last month, however, Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and DLK leader Ibrahim Rugova agreed on the return of Albanian students to official schools after a six-year boycott.

The wave of attacks coincides with press reports, confirmed by western diplomats in Belgrade, that a Serb-Albanian dialogue is to start next month in New York to resolve the status of Kosovo and its Albanians.

Although there has been no official confirmation has yet been made ahead of sensitive federal elections set for November 3, diplomats believe Serbia could set its human rights record straight by restoring some form of autonomy for the Albanians.
